.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 157 AM CDT Sat Sep 26 2026

A Rex block comprised of expansive ridging/high pressure over 
the Great Lakes, eastern Ontario, and southwestern Quebec and a 
deep coastal low/nor'easter just off the Mid-Atlantic coast will
lead to tranquil conditions here locally over the weekend and 
into early next week. Seasonable temperatures for late September
with highs in the mid 60s to mid 70s and lows in the mid 40s to
mid 50s can be expected while the blocking pattern is in place 
and keeps the same air mass locked in over the region.

One prominent shortwave presently over the central Plains will 
attempt to lift northeastward into the western Great Lakes 
tonight but will be stymied as it encounters the aforementioned 
Great Lakes ridge. A steady feed of dry low-mid-level air along 
the southern flank of the ridge should erode the associated 
shower activity as it attempts to enter our forecast area while 
its main forcing source is quickly weakened. A few of the latest
high-resolution model runs suggest that these showers/sprinkles
could get as far east as the I-39 corridor or so late tonight 
into Sunday morning before fading for good, though the majority 
of the latest forecast guidance generally favors this activity 
staying fenced off just to the west of our westernmost counties.

By midweek, the eastern CONUS Rex block will have broken down, 
allowing for a more progressive weather pattern to take shape. A
deep, positively-tilted longwave Pacific trough will evolve 
into a cut-off upper low over the Desert Southwest Monday into 
Tuesday, while a separate shortwave component of this trough 
breaks off and continues to progress towards the Great Lakes. As
this shortwave disturbance arrives in the region in tandem with
a frontal zone and an influx of column moisture, a period of 
rain appears likely to occur in our area sometime late Tuesday 
into Wednesday. There is a fair amount of ensemble support for 
a modest amount of instability building into our area during
this time period, suggesting that there could be some potential
for thunderstorms. However, this support is far from unanimous 
at this point.

How things will play out for late Wednesday and beyond will 
hinge heavily upon a complex interaction between the 
aforementioned upper low and the remnants of Pacific Hurricane 
Polo. Ensemble guidance broadly favors another period of rain 
(or perhaps just one, drawn-out period of rainfall beginning 
with the late Tuesday/Wednesday precipitation) occurring here 
during the latter half of the week as these atmospheric features
lift northeastward towards the Midwest and induce a poleward 
surge of combined Gulf and Pacific moisture. Unsurprisingly 
though, there is still quite a bit of spread across the latest 
global ensemble suites in exactly when any additional rainfall 
may occur here and how much rain we'll get. The broad-brushed 
chance and lower-end likely PoPs offered up by the NBM for the 
first few days of October thus seem to look appropriate for 
now.

While above normal temperatures will persist through the weekend, 
our upper level pattern will continue to experience changes over the 
next couple of days that will pave the way for widespread rain
chances and some cooler weather to finally arrive next week. 
Until then though, we will have to suffer through a few more days

Storm chances will return to western portions of the forecast area
this afternoon and evening as an approaching shortwave trough 
embedded in the northwest flow aloft results in the development 
of scattered showers and storms to our west/northwest. There are 
still some discrepancies amongst latest short-term guidance 
members, owing to weak forcing. The highest areas of uncertainty 
are (1) timing of storm development - with guidance split between 
late afternoon or early evening, and (2) how intense/widespread 
the convection will be. Both of these factors will have 
implications on storm chances overnight into Sunday morning. On 
the other hand, regardless of how these details play out, the

A similar set up to Saturday evening is expected again Sunday
evening, so there will be a chance for yet another round of 
scattered showers and storms. Should this round of showers and 
storms develop, it would be accompanied by an isolated severe 
weather threat, with hail and damaging winds expected to be the
main hazards.

Heading into early next week, we'll likely see a break from any 
rain chances before a more active pattern takes shape for the 
remainder of the period. A strong upper low will begin to traverse
the Southwest CONUS on Monday. This will have no effect on us just
yet, with hot and generally rain-free weather expected to prevail
prior to its arrival. 

Heading into the mid-week time period, we'll begin to see an 
increase in rain chances as the upper low begins its final 
approach. However, long-range guidance has yet to achieve a 
consensus on the evolution of the upper low. Some guidance is more
progressive, with rain chances beginning as early as Tuesday, 
while other guidance members are slower with the low's arrival, 
holding rain chances off until Wednesday or even Thursday. Given 
the uncertainty, the forecast will continue to evolve/change as a 
consensus is reached within the next few days. 

Aside from the timing discrepancies, widespread rain is expected
across the region once the upper low makes it's arrival.
Strengthening low level southerly winds are expected to tap into 
a plume of very rich Gulf moisture ahead of the upper low during
the middle of the week, which will set the stage for very 
efficient rainfall rates. The upper low will likely push a 
Pacific front towards the region mid to late week, which will 
serve as a focus for the development of widespread showers and 
thunderstorms. This front may not make it through the region, with
the cooler late-week temperatures more than likely a result of 
widespread rain/clouds. Multiple rounds of showers and 
thunderstorms will be possible through late week and even into the
weekend, depending on how long the upper low lingers over the 
region. Latest guidance suggests the arrival of a strong cold 
front will bring an end to our rainy/active period sometime next 
weekend, though this is certainly subject to change over the next
few days.

With all of this said, heavy rainfall is expected to be the main
concern throughout the week, given the potential for multiple
rounds of heavy rain. The threat for flash flooding will likely
increase with each round of showers and storms, despite our
rainfall deficit the past couple months or so. While it's still

monitoring over the next several days. While it's also still

as far north as Long Island before looping it southwestward
across New Jersey. As the pivot occurs, more rain will spread
into the area late tonight into Sunday. Chances will be highest
across the northern half of the area, and this period has the
highest chance for rain to reach as far west as the Alleghenies.
But the ultimate latitude of the low will have an impact on rain
amounts. While north central/northeast Maryland will likely see
the most rain regardless of the track, probabilities for 0.5
inch are much higher in the EC ensemble compared to the other
two ensembles.

Wind gusts will be 20-35 mph today, and up to 40 mph near the 
Chesapeake Bay. Winds any higher than that are becoming less 
likely. Similar or slightly lower winds are likely on Sunday,
with the highest values resulting from a farther southwest
and/or stronger low.

The warmest temperatures today (mid 70s) will be across the
Potomac Highlands and central Virginia as thicker clouds move in
from the east. On Sunday, clouds will envelop most of the area,
limiting highs to the 60s with 70s confined to central Virginia.

Coastal flooding, mostly minor in nature, will also be an 
issue...see separate section below.

While rain chances and wind gusts will likely start declining by
Monday, cloud cover will likely remain stubbornly in place. The
current forecast calls for upper 60s and lower 70s, but would
not be surprised if they are a bit lower if clouds are thick. 
As winds shift more northwesterly, some upslope showers or 
drizzle will be possible in the Alleghenies.
 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and calm conditions next week before 
rainfall chances return by late next week.

Generally benign weather conditions for the middle to late part of 
next week for our area. Upper troughing over the Northeast moves 
offshore Tuesday night into Wednesday, then a fast moving Clipper 
system passes by to our north Wednesday night into Thursday. Given 
all of the forcing remains to the north and moisture return ahead of 
the system is weak, not expecting any precip. Deep ridging develops 
over the southwest Atlantic at the end of next week, which brings in 
some warmer temperatures, but still not much in the way of moisture. 
The next chance for rain looks to be Friday into next weekend as a 
cold front approaches. Highs in the 70s for most of next week, 
though low 80s are possible in the middle to late part of the
week.

&&

A strong Nor'easter off the coast will bring gusty north to
northwest winds today and Sunday, with perhaps a modest decrease

Low levels have been trending drier through tonight, so while

not reduce visibility very much, and will likely fail to reach

tonight or Sunday as the low pivots near New Jersey. There's 
still some uncertainty with the extent of this rain, with CHO 
least likely to see any rain. MVFR ceilings will slowly spread
into the area as well, but this may not occur until Sunday
afternoon and evening.

Wind gusts and rain chances will decrease Sunday night into 
Monday, although MVFR ceilings will likely continue through
Monday night.

VFR conditions are forecast to prevail Tuesday and Wednesday, 
with no precipitation chances.

&&

As the Nor'easter churns offshore of the Delmarva coast, winds 
are expected to strengthen today. The Gale Warning has been
expanded to include the entire Chesapeake. While the western
waters will be farther removed from the wind fields, drier air
will promote deeper mixing, and some gale force gusts can't be
ruled out this afternoon. This situation will be monitored.
Winds should decrease slightly tonight, with Gale Warnings
ending at 10 PM this evening.

Exactly where the Nor'easter pivots near New Jersey could impact
winds on Sunday. While Small Craft Advisories are a sure bet, a
stronger/southwestward solution could result in another period
of gale conditions.

The Nor'easter will slowly pull away Monday, although Small

.DISCUSSION /Through Friday/...
Issued at 1110 PM MDT Fri Sep 25 2026

While most of today's activity has died down, we still have a few 
showers making their way across the eastern plains, and we expect 
them to continue weakening as they move east. As skies clear up and 
winds become light behind these showers, we could see some patchy 
fog develop in the northeastern counties for a few hours tonight.

Tomorrow and Sunday should both be much quieter weather days, thanks 
to subsidence from an upper-level ridge building over the area 
tonight into tomorrow. Zonal flow aloft from the ridge with some 
downsloping will bring some breezier conditions to the mountains and 
foothills in the early morning, with wind gusts of about 20-30 kts 
across the area and gusts up to 40 kts possible for the higher 
elevations. Dewpoints should drop into the 20s and 30s as the ridge 
moves into our CWA, and our high temperatures are expected to be in 
the mid 60s-70s for the mountains and low- to mid-80s for the 
plains. With both subsidence from the ridge and drier conditions at 
the surface, this weekend should stay dry and mostly sunny, though 
Sunday afternoon and evening could see a few showers over the 
mountains.

Models are trending slightly slower with the upper level trough/low 
next week. This has a few impacts on our potential weather for the
Monday through Thursday time period: One, the slower trough will 
push our better rain chances to later in the week, lowering our 
precip chances (and therefore snow chances) for the Monday and 
Tuesday time frame. Two, the slower track could allow for the 
remnants of Hurricane Polo to merge with the trough prior to it 
moving towards our area, which would give us better moisture and 
rain chances for late Tuesday through Wednesday. However, models 
are also trending a bit further south with the low, which will 
keep the best rain chances to the south/southeast of our forecast 
area. It also looks like the change in the positioning/timing of 
the upper low has impacted the strength of the cold front late 
Monday into Tuesday. The surface troughing and front are much 
weaker in the recent runs compared to those over the past few 
days. The weaker front and warmer temperatures will impact our 
snow chances Monday night/Tuesday morning in the higher terrain. 
Snow chances and amounts for this time period continue to 
decrease, with chances for at least a dusting of snow lowering 
into the 10% to 40% range for our higher mountain elevations 
(generally above 12,000ft now). 

For late Tuesday through Thursday, models have been pretty 
consistent with a swath of heavy rain developing, as moisture 
streams into the area and the upper low progresses from the SW 
U.S. into the central/south central U.S. However, the placement of
this swath varies from run to run. Similar to everything else, it
will depend on the evolution of the upper level system and 
surface low. Unfortunately for us, we look to be on the northern 
periphery of the higher rain totals, which means that there could 
be a pretty tight rainfall gradient somewhere over our forecast 
area (or potentially even just to the south of our area, missing 
us), where some people see multiple inches and others just a bit 
further north see tenths at most. The placement of this strong 
gradient will likely be the most difficult thing for us to 
forecast, and one of the most impactful parts of the forecast. The
speed of the upper level low will determine when the rain chances
end for us, with some members holding onto rain chances through 
early Friday, while others have us drying out Thursday.

toward the NJ coast the entire CWA should see the best push of

Peak of coastal flooding will be Saturday AM into Sunday AM

Saturday morning. Temperatures will gradually warm up through the

moisture starting later today and continuing through the remainder

expect a hot and slightly more humid Sunday with isolated diurnally-

least through Tuesday with isolated to scattered activity mainly in

lvl trough moves over the western CONUS and merges with the remnants 
of Polo. Confidence in a wetter pattern toward mid-late week 
continues to increase; however, confidence on timing, rain coverage,

climatological maximum for late September. However, most of them now 
keep the FROPA to our west. The GFS and its ensemble members 
continue to be the most progressive and aggressive solutions for our 
region, bringing periods of moderate to heavy rain through the end 
of the week. The ECMWF continues to be less aggressive and keeps the 
bulk of the QPF to our north/west. Overall, the probability of

for Wednesday, 50 to 60% for Thursday, and 30 to 40% on Friday. The 
probability of rain greater than 2 inches is slightly lower: 20-25% 
Wed, 30-45% Thurs, and 15 to 25% Fri. Given the spread in models 
regarding the evolution of this trough, and the eventual QPF, the 
main takeaway at the moment is to focus on impacts and not total 
amounts. Prepare for periods of showers and thunderstorms, mainly 
Wednesday into Friday. Finer details will be provided as confidence 
increases.

.SYNOPSIS...26/154 AM.

High temperatures will remain above normal through today with 
areas of low clouds and fog this morning. Substantial cooling is 
expected Sunday and Monday. Beach impacts from Tropical Cyclones 
well south of the region will be possible Monday and Tuesday in 
the form of high surf and possible beach erosion. A significant 
warming trend is expected Tuesday and Wednesday.

&&

.SHORT TERM (TDY-MON)...26/307 AM.

Not too much change in the forecast today compared to yesterday.
Only a few areas are seeing marine layer clouds this morning, and
really only South of Point Conception. These clouds may expand a
bit more by sunrise, but will be pretty limited to the coasts and
inland coasts thanks to some light offshore flow due to surface
pressure gradients trending offshore. These gradient trends are 
leading to a mini Santa Ana- like pattern for LA/Ventura, with 
light winds and 3-6 degrees warmer for these areas. High 
temperatures today for areas south of Point Conception/away from 
the coast will range in the 80s and to high 90s, with 
temperatures near the coast and north of Point Conception in the
70s and 80s. 

A bit of an odd situation synoptically starting Sunday, with quite
a bit of uncertainty. An upper level trough will start to drop 
into the region from the NW, and continue to move slowly through 
the region into next week. Meanwhile, two strong hurricanes are 
currently affecting the eastern Pacific (Polo and Odalys), well to
the south of California. There is quite a bit of uncertainty in 
the forecast due to the uncertainties in the evolution and tracks 
of these storms. The low pressure system may funnel some of the 
moisture from the into the region, however there is quite a spread
in the ensembles as some members show Precipitable Water values 
(PWATs) of 0.5 inches, and some show PWATs up to near 2 inches.
As a result, there may be possibility of light, spotty showers for
areas south of Point Conception starting Sunday. While the
official forecast does have a slight chance of rain for interior 
areas Sunday and Monday, there also is the possibility that most
of the moisture stays south of Los Angeles County. As for
temperatures, a cool down is expected Sunday and Monday with 
temperatures 10 to 20 degrees lower by Monday compared to today.

Ultimately, the biggest local impacts from the hurricanes to the 
south are still expected to be confined to the beaches with 
increasing swells from the hurricanes, though this is also quite 
uncertain pending the track of both hurricanes.

.LONG TERM (TUE-FRI)...26/310 AM.

Still a lot of uncertainty in the weather forecast Tuesday and 
beyond. More than 50 percent of the models are indicating high 
pressure building over the state behind the exitting trough, with
offshore flow and a fairly substantial warming trend through at 
least Thursday. There's at least a 30 to 40 percent chance of near
100 degree temperatures in the valleys and similar chances for 
Downtown LA and San Luis Obispo reaching 90 or higher. There's 
also a lower but still significant chance of temperatures 5-10 
degrees cooler than that. Will have to wait to see how the 
hurricanes track before having much confidence in the longer 
range.

&&

.AVIATION...26/1700Z.

At 1604Z at KLAX, the marine layer was 900 ft deep. The top of 
the inversion was at 2700 feet with a temperature of 25 Celsius.

High confidence in VFR TAFs for KPRB, KBUR, KVNY, KWJF, and KPMD.

highest for KLAX/KLGB/KSMO. South of Point Conception cigs would 
likely be patchy and may frequently bounce between SCT and BKN if
they form.

flight cat thereafter. 40% chance for BKN007-012 conds 10Z-17Z.
If cigs form they may bounce between BKN and SCT frequently.

Moderate to high confidence in TAF through 18Z Sat and
after 03Z Sun, otherwise high confidence. CIGs may scatter and 
reform several times due to high level clouds this morning. There
is a 30% chance of BKN008-012 CIGs after 03Z Sun. High confidence
in no significant east win component.

KBUR...High confidence in VFR TAF.

&&

.MARINE...26/840 AM.

Through this weekend, moderate to high confidence in Small Craft 
Advisory (SCA) winds and steep seas affecting the outer waters. 
The current SCAs will likely be extended through Tuesday night.
Gale force gusts will be possible at times, especially Monday 
afternoon and evening across the southern waters. Nearshore along
the Central coast will see SCA winds and steep seas this 
afternoon into evening.

Moderate to high confidence in widespread gusty winds Monday into
Tuesday extending into the nearshore waters at times, with the
highest confidence in the Central Coast waters and Santa Barbara
Channel.

Southerly swells from Hurricanes Odalys (SSW) and Polo (SSE) will
affect the region this weekend through the middle of next week. 
These swells will create larger waves and surf nearshore, which 
could impact some harbor entrances, especially Sunday through 
Tuesday.

&&

.BEACHES...26/858 AM.

Southerly swells from Hurricanes Odalys and Polo will affect the 
waters this weekend through the middle of next week. This is a 
complex scenario with two hurricanes so close in proximity, with 
one of them (Odalys) poorly handled by our computer models. 
Another complexity is the relatively short window of time that 
Polo is far enough west for its waves to have a clear path to
southern California. This means that the swells will have a 
narrow window of time to line up with the high tides. Lastly, some
south-facing shores are extra vulnerable because of the lingering
erosion effects from Hurricane Marie earlier this month. 

While the surf heights will likely be in the 4 to 7 foot range 
for south facing beaches Sunday through Tuesday, there is a plus 
or minus in that potential of 2 feet or so due to the 
complications mentioned above. High tides will steadily build each
day and peak Monday and Tuesday, likely reaching around 7 feet 
(MLLW) - which is higher by almost a foot over astronomical tides 
due to ongoing effects of El Nino. 

There is a significant concern of Coastal Flooding over vulnerable
south-facing beaches as a result, but the magnitude is still 
uncertain. The areas of most concern include Avalon, Long Beach, 
Malibu and Santa Barbara. The reasonable worst-case scenario is 
for impacts similar to those from Hurricane Marie, but the most 
likely outcome is for impacts to be a step less. The one exception
being Avalon on Catalina Island, as the swells from Hurricane 
Polo will be more from a southeasterly direction than with Marie, 
which they are more exposed to. The same goes for Santa Barbara 
Harbor where the risk is less but still present. 

South-facing beaches should plan for shallow flooding of seawater
over low lying beach walkways, parking lots, and roads as well as
potential for significant beach erosion. Very localized damage to
structures is also possible in the most vulnerable areas. With 
all that stated, there is a potential that impacts will be minimal
if the lower-end surf outcome materializes.

Due to rather high uncertainty, the Beach Hazard Statements will
continue through Wednesday afternoon. This covers the coastline 
from Santa Barbara South coast down to LA county, including 
Catalina island. A decision to upgrade to Coastal Flood Advisory 
will be made today or Sunday.

The next upper level system and associated trough axis will race 
across Canada and Northern Plains through the short term. In 
response to said upper level system, low level flow will increase 
out of the south, advecting moisture across the region. 
Ensemble guidance shows precipitable water values 150-200 
percent of normal overlaying the region through the day with DP 
temps in the mid to upper 50s to around 60 degrees across 
western MN. As a result, rain chances increase this morning with
scattered to widespread showers. High res model guidance 
depicts this swath of showers moving SW to NE through the 
morning, bringing it into the metro by 10am(SW metro) to 
12pm(NE metro) timeframe. Shower activity will be more 
widespread across western MN, with lesser probabilities and 
coverage across eastern MN and western WI. Expected rainfall 
amounts will range from 0.30-0.70 inches across western MN and 
less than 0.30 inches across eastern MN and western WI. Forecast
soundings show a sliver of elevated CAPE across western MN, 
can't rule out a rumble of thunder embedded within the shower 
activity. High temperatures on Saturday will trend cooler with 
highs in the low to middle 60s, middle to upper 60s across 
western/central WI.

On Sunday, the aforementioned upper level system and associated 
moisture will quickly translate east. Upper level ridge axis 
will settle in it's wake across the region with dry conditions 
expected throughout the day, a remnant isolated shower or two 
possible during the morning hours. High temperatures rebound 
back up into the upper 60s. Surface high pressure will settle in
over the Great Lakes region. Being on the western periphery, 
southerly flow will remain in place, with DP temps remaining 
around 60 degrees.

On Monday, south/southwesterly flow will remain locked in across the 
region ahead of the next upper level shortwave trough. High 
temperatures will warm a few degrees from Sunday, around 70 degrees 
areawide. With anomalous moisture in place, the next upper level 
shortwave and associated surface front will promote scattered to
widespread showers and embedded thunderstorms on Tuesday. As of
now, there's still a degree of uncertainty regarding how this 
system evolves. That said, it's to difficult, with not the best 
forecaster confidence to determine exact rainfall totals. But 
the one trend that is remaining fairly consistent is lesser rain
totals as most of the upper level forcing and dynamics hone in 
across far northern MN and south into the IA/MO/NE/IL region. 
Looking at 00z deterministic models and their respected ensemble
suites, guidance is painting greater than 60 percent 
chance(medium to high confidence) of 24 hour rainfall totals of 
greater than 0.10 inches areawide. Looking at the probability of
24 hour totals greater than 0.50 inches, guidance is painting 
at 10-40 percent chance(low to medium confidence).

The next chance for rain will be on Thursday. An upper level trough 
will move across the Desert Southwest before ejecting northeastward 
across the Plains and towards the Upper Midwest. There still remains 
uncertainty regarding this system, and how far north the associated 
deep and anomalous moisture advects. That said, 15-30 percent PoPs 
remain in the forecast grids, highlighting Thursday rain 
chances.

KEY MESSAGE 1...A developing Nor'easter east of the Mid-Atlantic
coast lifts to the north, then retrogrades back towards New Jersey
over the weekend before finally departing on Tuesday. This will
bring periods of rain and strong winds at the coast to the region.

Broad high pressure remains centered over eastern Canada and extends
back into the Great Lakes. While the high will weaken and lift into
northern portions of the Province of Quebec, it will still be strong
enough to create a tight pressure gradient between it and low pressure
east of the Mid-Atlantic. The trend with the last run of models has
been to bring the storm closer to the shore, and even have the center
of the Nor'easter move into New Jersey Saturday night. 

A tight north to northeast pressure gradient develops tonight and
will persist through the weekend as this Nor'easter retrogrades
back towards New Jersey Saturday through Saturday night. Winds 
increase tonight, generally to 25 to 35 mph with 40 to 50 mph 
inland, and gusts up to 60 mph at the coast. Will keep High Wind
Warnings and Wind Advisories in effect through Saturday night, 
but additional headlines may be needed on Sunday depending on 
the strength and position of the low on Sunday. This trend may 
result in stronger winds farther west as well. Given that trees 
still have their leaves, the combination of these winds and 
heavy rain (more on that in a bit) will result in tree damage, 
as well as power line and potentially roof damage with highest 
impacts at the coast.

The farther inland trend also results in higher PoPs inland as well
as and higher rainfall over the area. Rain spreads into the region
from east to west through Saturday. PoPs will be 60 to 70 
percent across the southern Poconos, Lehigh Valley, and far 
northwest New Jersey and 80 to 90 percent across the rest of New
Jersey, southeast Pennsylvania, and Delmarva. PoPs will then be
90 to 100 percent across the whole area Saturday night and 
Sunday. Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches of QPF along the I-95 
corridor and points north and west with as much as 3 inches 
over much of eastern New Jersey with locally heavier amounts 
possible. This will be over a 48 to 60 hour timeframe, so 
widespread flooding is nor anticipated at this time, though 
there may be some flooding concerns by late Sunday and Sunday 
night. In addition, runoff from this rain may exacerbate coastal
flooding, which will be covered by Coastal Flood Warnings. 
Cannot rule out a few embedded thunderstorms, mainly at the 
coast, during this time.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Multiple rounds of significant tidal flooding 
expected into this weekend. Major Coastal Flood levels are now
expected for the New Jersey Atlantic Coast, the Delaware 
Atlantic Coast, and portions of central and southern Delaware 
Bay.

With a slow moving nor'easter and multiple days of strong 
northeast winds expected, the confidence in the threat for tidal
flooding remains high. In fact, the threat for the New Jersey
Atlantic Coast, Delaware Atlantic Coast, and portions of
southern Delaware Bay to reach Major Flood levels around the 
time of high tide Saturday morning has increased once again, so
we have increased the forecast for these areas to exceed Major 
Flood levels. Strong onshore flow that has persisted for several
days is resulting in water piling up across tidal tributaries 
and within back bays of coastal communities. Tidal levels will 
also be enhanced with astronomical tides increasing with the 
upcoming Full Moon Saturday. 

For Delaware Bay communities, north/northeast winds will keep 
pushing water to the west side of the Bay and onto the Delaware 
coast. This will increase the forecast for Major Flood levels 
around southern and central Delaware. The Coastal Flood Warning 
remains 2 AM Sunday for Kent and Sussex, DE. Moderate Flood 
levels are forecasted for Cumberland and Salem, NJ as well as 
New Castle, DE, so the Warning remains across these areas.

For the tidal Delaware River, widespread minor tidal flooding 
continues to be forecast, so the Coastal Flood Advisory remains
in effect through Saturday Night for the tidal Delaware River. 
While not currently expected, we cannot rule out Moderate tidal
flooding getting to Delaware River communities. 

As mentioned above, more north/northeasterly winds will limit 
the tidal flooding threat for the Chesapeake Bay. Some spotty 
minor tidal flooding is anticipated at Claiborne, but nothing 
higher than that at this time. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Dangerous rip currents and high surf are 
expected at the Jersey Shore and Delaware Beaches through 
Sunday. Beach erosion is likely and breaching of sand dunes is 
possible.

A nor'easter off our coast will bring strong north to northeast
winds and high seas for our marine zones. Breaking waves within
the surf zone of 6 to 12 feet are expected through Sunday. 
Dangerous rip currents will accompany the high surf, making it 
extremely dangerous to enter the water at any time through 
Sunday. The high surf and strong winds will likely result in 
areas of beach erosion across the Jersey Shore and Delaware 
Beaches. Large breaking waves in the surf zone and high water 
levels may result in breaching of sand dunes.

The High Risk for life threatening rip currents remains in effect
through Sunday for all beaches. A High Surf Advisory is in effect
for all beaches through Sunday as well.

Area Forecast Discussion

.UPDATE...Updated 12Z Aviation Discussion.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...

- For tonight into Sunday, higher level moisture will surge back
  into the region with skies becoming cloudy and eventual chances
  for light rain later in the day on Sunday. 

- Rain is likely across much of Arizona on Monday and Tuesday with
  the possibility of some strong to severe thunderstorms. Moderate
  to heavy rainfall will also be possible, particularly across 
  the Arizona high terrain.

- Temperatures will cool to below normal during the first half of
  next week with highs only in the eighties for much of the lower
  deserts.
 
&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH SUNDAY/... 
The main forecast concern continues to be the potential for strong
to severe storms, heavy rainfall, and flash flooding early next
week.  

However, in the short term quiet weather conditions will continue
today as westerly flow persists. Expect mostly sunny skies today 
with a slight uptick in temperatures as afternoon highs top out in
the upper 90s in the Phoenix area to the lower 100s across the 
western lower deserts. 

This will all begin to change tonight into Sunday as upper level 
moisture gets peeled away from the decaying TC Odalys and advected
into our region. We should expect higher level clouds 
overspreading the area from the southwest starting this evening, 
gradually thickening up tonight with cloud bases dropping more 
into the mid levels Sunday morning. The moisture advection will be
aided by a Pacific trough which is forecast to dive southeastward
toward the northern California coast on Sunday. There is still 
some question for rain chances on Sunday as considerable dry air 
will still be present in the lower levels. We do expect this 
stream of moisture to last long enough to result in decent top 
down saturation with light rain eventually reaching the surface, 
but only in narrow bands. PoPs gradually increase from 10-15% 
chances Sunday afternoon to 30-40% after midnight Sunday night. 
Most areas that do see measurable rainfall on Sunday should stay 
under 0.05". Daytime highs Sunday will also be held down due to 
the cloudy skies with NBM forecast highs mostly in the mid 90s, 
but it would not be surprising to struggle to make it past the 
lower 90s. 

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/... 
Model guidance is still pointing toward the potential for a
significant weather event occurring early next week as a strong
Pacific low pressure system moves into the region at the same time
moisture from TC Polo is forecast to advect northward into
Arizona. There have been some changes within the model runs over 
the last 24 hours, noticeably with the low deepening further on 
Monday and potentially becoming a slow moving closed low for 
Tuesday into early Wednesday. The latest NHC track of Polo still 
keeps it well to our south and southeast with its eventual remnant
circulation missing Arizona. However, it is still expected to 
heavily influence our low and mid level moisture which will be one
of the key ingredients needed for a big rainfall event.

Model clusters heavily favor a closed low forming to our northwest
going into Monday with further strengthening possible as it moves
into our region on Tuesday. This deepening would result in a 
slower moving system which has pushed back the timing of the best
rain chances, now most likely occurring late Monday night and/or 
on Tuesday. Scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms are still
expected during the first half of Monday, but they should favor 
the central and eastern Arizona high terrain. Pockets of moderate 
rainfall will also be possible Monday, but the heavy rainfall 
threat seems to have pushed back to Monday night and Tuesday. WPC 
still maintains a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall for Monday 
and Monday night for most of Arizona, minus the southwestern 
portion. 

Assuming no big changes with the timing and the strength of the
low, Tuesday now looks to hold our best chances for widespread
rainfall, likely moderate to heavy at times, and potentially a few
discrete severe thunderstorms. As the Pacific low slowly moves
into our region, strong 35-55 kt mid level south to southwesterly
flow will support very good upslope forced ascent into central and
eastern Arizona. At the same time, we are expecting to fall under
strong difluence aloft from as early as Monday evening through
Tuesday evening. One of the more uncertain ingredients for the 
severe storm potential is the amount of instability that will be
available. Although model guidance suggests CAPE will struggle to
top 500 J/kg, it seems very possible a narrow corridor of better
instability closer to 1000 J/kg may develop later on Tuesday. If
all the ingredients come together, a few severe storms producing 
damaging winds and large hail will be possible. 

The latest QPF amounts have risen over the south-central Arizona
lower deserts with average amounts closer to 1.0" in the Phoenix
area to anywhere from 0.15-0.5" across the western lower deserts.
The highest storm total rainfall amounts are expected over the
high terrain north and east of Phoenix with current forecast 
average amounts of 1-2". Locally higher amounts will occur due to 
training of showers and storms with some areas potentially 
reaching 3" for the two day period. The latest NBM guidance shows 
probabilities of 2" as high as 55% for the higher terrain north 
and east of Phoenix to 20% within Phoenix. NBM probabilities of 
getting 3" of rainfall lower to 10-20% for higher terrain areas. 
We will have to wait and see if these rainfall probabilities hold,
although even at this point it seems quite likely Flood Watches 
will be needed for later Monday and Tuesday.

Due to the likely deeper and slower progression of the Pacific 
low, rain chances now extend through Tuesday night for the eastern
half of Arizona and we anticipate PoPs to increase on Wednesday 
if the timing holds. Any rainfall Tuesday night and Wednesday
should be more scattered, but we can't rule out a few
thunderstorms producing additional localized moderate rainfall. 
If the cold core of the low hangs out over our area into Wednesday
afternoon, we could easily see some afternoon storms that produce
small hail. For the western portions of our area on Wednesday,
drier air is expected to quickly move in leaving clearing skies 
and quiet conditions.

Temperatures during the first part of next week will definitely
cool off with highs falling into the 80s for the south-central
Arizona lower deserts to the upper 80s and lower 90s for the
western lower deserts. After the Pacific low finally ejects to the
east late week, upper level ridging is favored to move in from the
west leading to gradual warming with highs potentially reaching
100 degrees again by next weekend.

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1125Z. 

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT: 
No aviation weather concerns are expected through the forecast
period. Winds will follow light and diurnal trends with some
variability prior to directional shifts. A period of southerly
crosswinds (150v200) is also anticipated at KPHX and KDVT late 
this morning/early afternoon prior to the westerly shift. High 
clouds will gradually increase in coverage through tonight.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH: 
No aviation concerns are expected during the next 24 hours. Winds
will fluctuate between westerly and southeasterly at KIPL and
southerly to southwesterly at KBLH. Wind speeds at both terminals
will remain aob 10 kt. Gradually increasing high clouds can be
expected through this morning with mid level cloud decks starting
to move into the region late in the period. 

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
Dry conditions will prevail today before higher level moisture
moves in on Sunday resulting in chances for mostly light rain.  
MinRHs today will bottom out today at 15-20% across the lower
deserts to 20-30% over the eastern Arizona high terrain. Slow
improvement in RHs is expected on Sunday before much higher 
moisture levels move in on Monday as rain chances quickly 
increase and expand. Winds will generally follow the typical 
diurnal tendencies with limited to no afternoon gusts this 
weekend. Rain and much cooler weather are expected for Monday and
Tuesday with heavy rainfall a decent possibility across the 
eastern districts. Conditions should eventually dry out later 
next week with temperatures returning to near normal.

Pockets of MVFR have developed this morning across the Napa River

depth of this moisture is shallow per our presently ascending 
weather balloon from OAK and should translate to clearing roughly

indication that VFR may not return today. A storm system will

1,000-1,500 ft) to around 12,000 ft is minimal. However, 
noteworthy lift will translate to moistening of this layer with a 
potential for weak convection capable of pockets of turbulence and
virga below FL120.

return by 18Z today. Winds today are anticipated to be a bit more

MVFR cigs push, with another cig, albeit VFR, around FL120. 
Virga/turbulence below cloud base cannot be ruled out.

from PAO and SQL, though it appears that areas near SJC will
remain SKC. Clearing is expected by the 17Z-18Z time frame. 

Monterey Bay Terminals...Remnant turbulence in the wake of Friday's 
cold front has disrupted fog development and the current TAF set is 
slightly more optimistic, especially at KSNS. Occasional IFR 
stratus is still anticipated to persist through at least the 15Z

stronger onshore flow and result in MVFR ceilings. While guidance

struggle to re-develop after a couple of days of dry continental 
flow and it's probable that this initial surge will be 
intermittent. The current TAF set estimates that the best window 
for more persistent cigs to be closer to 04Z. MVFR will prevail 
through sunrise Sunday. While the potential for IFR is too low to 
include at this juncture, it's non-zero and we'll monitor trends 
in guidance for potential inclusion in subsequent TAF issuances.

Fresh to strong northerly breezes are forecast to continue

conditions, especially for waters beyond 10 nautical miles from

Our diffuse cold front continues to slowly move southward through

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1... 
Sunday and Monday will feature much more in the way of cloud 
cover than the past two days as mid and upper level moisture 
associated with the Nor'easter moves westward. As of now, there 
is a low chance /<25%/ of measurable precipitation mainly east 
of I-79. Can not rule out sprinkles as far west as I-77 Sunday 
night into Monday. 

This won't be a washout in any area, but with mostly cloudy to an 
overcast sky, temperatures during the day pull back into the mid and 
upper 60s save for areas west of I-77 who will see more
sunshine. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Come tuesday night, clouds associated with the nor'easter will 
be out of our area. This allows a transitory H5 ridge axis to 
move in returning dry and warmer weather. Thursday will be the 
warmest day of the week with widespread 70s. Latest probs of 
maxT 80F or greater continue to increase for northern WV, 
southeastern OH, and southwestern PA as they now reside between 
40-60%. This by no means is near record territory as benchmarks 
for 1 October are still near 90F at most climate sites. Heat 
risk at this juncture remains in the minor category. 

We reside just south of a baroclinic zone which is along Lake Erie 
into upstate New York placing us in the warm sector Friday and 
Saturday. The trend continues for dry weather, however a weak 
impulse could traverse generating scattered showers.  For now, probs 
between 20-40% have been consistent in the warm sector.  With 
increased moisture in the column, forecast highs pull back a little 
on day 6 and 7 to the lower to mid 70s, while overnight lows near 60 
are projected with above average confidence. 

For locations who do not receive rainfall Sunday night or Monday 
then none is expected the balance of September.

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Confidence remains high that VFR conditions will prevail through
this evening under high pressure. A Nor'easter currently offshore
southern New Jersey/Delmarva Peninsula will continue to track 
north over the next 12 hours before turning to the northwest
helping to maintain northerly to northeasterly flow across our 
region through Monday. Due to stronger low-level flow drifting 
west on the periphery of the nor'easter, flow aloft will be 
stronger late tonight which could lend to some brief periods of
low-level wind shear at the eastern terminals (DUJ and LBE).

ZZV and MGW could keep partly cloudy skies overnight which 
could result in river-valley fog development, however, there is
high uncertainty of any development. Light rain is possible 
tomorrow as early as the afternoon for DUJ and LBE, however, it
is more likely to start during the evening. The chance for MVFR
will gradually increase for terminals from east to west as the 
nor'easter moves onshore. There is >50% of at least MVFR 
ceilings region-wide by Monday morning.

Outlook...
There is about a 35%-50% chance of IFR ceilings Monday morning 
for FKL, DUJ, and LBE. Restrictions will briefly improve during 
the day on Monday. Tuesday morning there is a chance for 
restrictions during the morning, otherwise conditions will 
remain VFR until the next disturbance moves in mid to late week.
